title: Heat and Cold
intro: Heat waves and cold snaps do most of their harm indoors, above all when the power or the heating fails. This module sets up one room you can keep livable, tells you when to leave for somewhere safer, and covers heating safely, with the carbon monoxide alarm that goes with it.

actions.title: Put a thermometer in the room you sleep in
actions.why: People misjudge indoor heat and cold, most of all at night, and a number on the wall tells you when to act.
actions.how: Place an easy-to-read thermometer at about head height, out of direct sun and away from the stove and heaters. PreparedBC's Extreme Heat Guide gives two indoor figures for vulnerable people: risk rises once the room is above 79 °F (26 °C), and 88 °F (31 °C) or more is dangerous, above all if the room does not cool down at night. Vulnerable here means older adults, people who live alone, people with heart or lung disease, diabetes or mental illness, pregnant people, babies and young children, and people with limited mobility. In a heat wave or a cold spell, read it in the morning, late afternoon and at bedtime.
actions.done: An easy-to-read thermometer is in place in the room you sleep in, out of direct sun and away from heaters, and it shows a reading.

actions.title: Pick your cool room
actions.why: With limited cooling, keeping one room cool is achievable where keeping a whole home cool is not.
actions.how: Choose the room that is usually coolest: on the lowest floor you have, on the shaded side, with the fewest or smallest sun-facing windows. Plan to cool only that room and to move both sleeping and daytime living into it during a heat wave: mattresses or mats, the thermometer, drinking water, a lamp and chargers. Check your choice by reading the thermometer there on a hot evening, because indoor heat peaks at about 9 to 10 p.m.
actions.done: Everyone at home can point to the cool room, and you have read the thermometer there on one hot evening.

actions.title: Shade your windows, from the outside if you can
actions.why: Keeping the sun off the glass can lower the temperature indoors by about 4 to 5 °F (2 to 3 °C).
actions.how: For each window that gets direct sun, put shade on the outside if you can: an awning, shutters, shade cloth on a balcony, or even cardboard fixed over the outside of the window. Where you cannot, cut cardboard to the size of the pane, cover one side in aluminum foil, and stand it inside the window with the foil facing out; add thick or lined curtains and keep them closed by day. Make the panels now, label each with its window, and store them flat.
actions.done: Each window that gets direct sun has outside shade in place, or a labeled foil-and-cardboard panel made for it and stored flat.
actions.apartment: Leases and building rules often forbid fixing anything to the outside, and nothing must be able to fall from a height, so most apartment households use balcony shade or the foil-and-cardboard panels inside the glass.

actions.title: Close up by day and open up at night
actions.why: Heat builds up indoors over several days, and shutting it out by day and letting cooler air in at night is the main way to slow that.
actions.how: In a heat wave, keep windows, outside doors, blinds and curtains closed from about 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. From about 8 p.m., once the air outside is cooler than the air inside, open the windows and run fans, including the kitchen and bathroom exhaust fans, to pull the cooler air through. Close up again in the morning before it warms. If the air is smoky, read AR-07 before opening windows. If your windows do not open, or open only a few inches (HR-24 has you check), night air cannot cool the home: plan to spend the hottest hours in a cool place (HC-07), leave earlier in a heat wave, and write that on the Our reasons to leave sheet.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the routine, and if your windows cannot let night air in, leaving earlier is written on the Our reasons to leave sheet.

actions.title: Stop counting on fans in high heat
actions.why: A fan moves air but does not lower body temperature, so it can feel like relief while the body keeps heating up.
actions.how: Do not use a fan as your main way of keeping cool: fans do not prevent heat illness in people at higher risk, at any temperature. Once the room is above 90 °F (32 °C) a fan can raise body temperature, so switch to cooling your skin with water (HC-06) or leave for a cool place (HC-07). Keep fans for one job: pulling cooler air in at night (HC-04).
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the fan rule and can name the two things you do instead.

actions.title: Cool your body, not the room, when the power is out
actions.why: With no air conditioning, water on the skin and water to drink are the cooling you have left, and the signs of heat illness tell you when that is no longer enough.
actions.how: Put a wet cloth on your neck, wear a damp shirt or sleep under a damp sheet, and take a cool shower, bath or foot bath; a basin of stored water works when the faucets are dry. Drink water through the day whether or not you feel thirsty (if you are on a fluid limit or take water pills, ask your clinician how much). Watch everyone for the signs of heat exhaustion and heat stroke, and act on them the moment you see them (X7-01).
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the ways to cool down with water.

actions.title: List the cool places you can walk to
actions.why: A few hours somewhere air-conditioned lets the body recover, and in a heat wave you will not want to be hunting for addresses.
actions.how: Find three air-conditioned places within a walk or a short ride: a library, a shopping mall, a community center, a movie theater, a place of worship, a friend or relative, or one of your city's official cooling centers. Write each address and its opening hours by hand on the printable Our reasons to leave sheet, and include one that is open in the evening. Agree your trigger: anyone at higher risk goes when the room reaches 88 °F (31 °C), and everyone goes at the first signs of heat illness (X7-01). The figure is a line for leaving, not a promise that the room is safe below it: with a baby, follow FN-05, which does not wait for a number. Take water with you.
actions.done: Three cool places, one open in the evening, are on the Our reasons to leave sheet with addresses and hours, and everyone at home has agreed the trigger.

actions.title: Pair up with a heat buddy
actions.why: People who live alone are among those most at risk in a heat wave, and a check from someone else catches trouble they may not notice themselves.
actions.how: Agree with a neighbor, friend or relative that during any heat warning you will check on each other at least twice a day, by a knock or a call, with one check in the late afternoon or evening when homes are hottest. Agree that either of you will take the other to a cool place (HC-07) if it is needed. Write each other's numbers by hand on the printable emergency numbers sheet. When you check, look for the signs of heat illness and act on them (X7-01).
actions.done: Your heat buddy has said yes to checking on each other in a heat warning, and their number is written on your emergency numbers sheet.

actions.title: Store extra drinking water for hot weather
actions.why: Ready.gov says water needs can double in very hot temperatures, so the usual allowance of a gallon a day is a baseline, not a hot-weather figure.
actions.how: On top of your normal stock (U4-02), add up to one more gallon per person for each day of a heat wave you want to cover; the site works this out from your household setup and shows the extra amount, not the normal stock. Keep a few quarts more for wetting cloths and a foot bath (HC-06). In heat, drink through the day without waiting for thirst; if you are on a fluid limit or take water pills, ask your clinician how much to drink.
actions.done: The extra water the site works out for your household is stored at home on top of your normal stock.

actions.title: Find the cooler spots lower in your building
actions.why: Upper floors and sun-facing units are often the hottest homes in a building, and the lowest floor out of the sun is usually the coolest.
actions.how: On a hot afternoon, take your thermometer to the lobby, a lower hallway, a shaded common room and the shaded side of the building, and note which is coolest. Ask management whether a common room on a low floor can be opened as a cool room in a heat wave. If you live high up, plan to spend the hottest hours, late afternoon to late evening, in the coolest spot you found, and allow for the climb back if the elevators are out.
actions.done: You have walked the building with your thermometer on a hot afternoon, everyone at home can name the coolest spot, and management has answered your question about a cool room.

actions.title: Ask how your medicines behave in heat
actions.why: Some medicines change how the body copes with heat or loses water, and some are damaged by a hot room.
actions.how: At your next pharmacy visit, or by phone, ask three questions about everything you take: does any of it raise my risk in hot weather; how much should I drink (this matters most if you are on a fluid limit or take water pills); and how should I store it if my home gets hot. Do not stop or change a medicine without advice. Write the answers by hand on your printable medication list.
actions.done: The pharmacist's answers to the three questions are written on your medication list.

actions.title: Take children and pets with you every time you park
actions.why: A parked car heats up so fast that a child left inside can die within minutes.
actions.how: Never leave a child, a pet or anyone who cannot get out alone in a parked car, not for a minute and not with a window open. Put your phone or bag on the back seat so that you always open the back door before you lock up. Keep the parked car locked and the keys out of reach so that children cannot climb in. If you see a child alone in a car, call 911 (or your local emergency number).
actions.done: Every driver at home has heard the rule, and a phone or bag now goes on the back seat on every trip.

actions.title: Set up one air-conditioned room if you can
actions.why: One cooled room gives everyone in the household a place to recover, which is enough to keep people safe through a heat wave.
actions.how: Install a window or portable air conditioner in your cool room (HC-02) and keep the door closed so that it only has to cool that room. It does not need to run at full strength to keep you safe: PreparedBC's Extreme Heat Guide treats 79 °F (26 °C) as the point where risk starts to rise for vulnerable people, so set it to hold the room below that. Check your lease and your window type first, because many apartment windows only take a portable unit with a hose. It will not run in an outage, so keep HC-06 and HC-07 as your backup.
actions.done: A window or portable air conditioner is installed in your cool room, your lease allows it, and it has cooled the room with the door closed.

actions.title: Pick your warm room
actions.why: With the heating off, one small closed room holds body warmth far better than a whole home does.
actions.how: Choose the smallest room that everyone can sleep in, with the fewest windows, away from the side the wind hits; a room with no outside wall is best. Plan to shut the doors to every room you do not need, push a rolled towel against the gap under the warm room's door, and bring everyone, pets included, into that one room. Decide now where the bedding, warm clothes, lights and water will go.
actions.done: Everyone at home can point to the warm room and to where the bedding, warm clothes, lights and water for it are kept.

actions.title: Insulate the warm room
actions.why: Covering the glass and blocking drafts keeps more of your body heat in the room.
actions.how: Before winter, put a clear window-film kit over the windows of your warm room (HC-14), following the instructions on the package. In a cold outage, hang blankets over the windows at night and take them down by day wherever the sun shines in. Push rolled towels against the gaps under doors and around drafty frames. Keep the door you would leave by easy to open.
actions.done: Clear window film is in place over each window of the warm room, and the door you would leave by still opens easily.

actions.title: Dress indoors as you would outdoors
actions.why: Clothing is the one source of warmth that needs no power, and catching hypothermia early depends on someone knowing the signs.
actions.how: Wear several loose, light, warm layers in place of one thick one, with a hat, dry wool socks and mittens; take a layer off before you sweat and change anything that gets damp. Watch each other for the signs of hypothermia, and act on them at once (X7-01).
actions.done: Each person has warm layers, a hat, wool socks and mittens in one known place.

actions.title: Sleep in a small space inside the warm room
actions.why: A smaller space around your body holds on to the heat you give off through the night.
actions.how: Give each person a sleeping bag whose comfort rating, not the number in its name, is 32 °F (0 °C) or lower, or a stack of several blankets. A bag sold as a '20' is often comfortable only to the mid-30s, so plan a blanket over it. Put a mat, cushions or folded blankets underneath, because a cold floor draws heat away. To go further, pitch a small tent on the bed or floor, or drape blankets over a table or chairs, and sleep close together inside. Never bring a candle, stove or heater into it. A baby does not sleep in a sleeping bag or inside the blanket shelter with others: they need a safe sleep space of their own, so follow FN-05 for babies.
actions.done: The sleeping bags or blankets and the mats this action calls for are stored in or near the warm room, one set for each person who will use one.

actions.title: Rule out ovens, stovetops, grills and camp stoves for heating
actions.why: Anything that burns fuel gives off carbon monoxide, which builds up unseen in a closed room and kills more than 400 people a year in the United States.
actions.how: Never heat your home with an oven, a gas stovetop, a charcoal or gas grill, a camp stove, a patio heater, a clothes dryer, candles, or any kerosene, propane, butane or other fuel heater that has no flue to the outside. The same goes for a generator, or a car running in a garage. Have a working carbon monoxide alarm (HC-22). If the alarm sounds, or people have a headache, dizziness, weakness, an upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain or confusion, get everyone out into fresh air and call 911 (or your local emergency number) from there.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the rule, and your carbon monoxide alarm sounds when you press its test button.
actions.apartment: In an apartment this rule has no exceptions: no fuel-burning heater or stove of any kind for heat, indoors or on the balcony.

actions.title: Know your only safe heat without grid power
actions.why: Once fuel-burning heaters are ruled out, it helps to know what is left, and how little a battery can do, before a cold night forces a bad choice.
actions.how: Your safe heat in a cold outage is body heat held in by layers (HC-16), a small insulated room (HC-14, HC-15) and a sleeping bag or blanket shelter (HC-17). A battery adds only a little: as an estimate, a 1,500-watt electric heater empties a 1,000 Wh power station in about half an hour, while a 60-watt electric blanket or heated throw runs for about 14 hours, so use a power station for a heated throw, never a room heater. When the power is back and you run an electric heater, keep it 3 feet from anything that can burn and switch it off when you leave the room or go to sleep. If this is not enough to keep people warm, leave for a warm place (HC-21).
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard this action read aloud and can say what your safe heat is when the power is off.
actions.apartment: No fuel-burning heater belongs in an apartment, including models sold as safe for indoor use.

actions.title: Protect your pipes in a freeze
actions.why: A frozen pipe can burst and flood your home, and the homes below it, when it thaws.
actions.how: Before winter, find the valves that shut off your home's water (U2-97) and ask management how the building's pipes are protected and who to call after hours. In a hard freeze, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls so that room air reaches the pipes. If a faucet stops running or you see a leak, shut the water off at your valves (in a house, at the main) and call management or a plumber at once. Never thaw a pipe with a blowtorch or any other open flame, or with a fuel-burning heater.
actions.done: You can point to your home's water shut-off valves, and management has told you how the pipes are protected and who to call after hours.
actions.apartment: The pipes in the walls belong to the building, so your part is your own unit's valves and a fast report to management.

actions.title: List the warm places you can reach
actions.why: Spending the coldest hours somewhere heated is the safest answer to a home you cannot keep warm.
actions.how: Find two or three heated places you could reach on foot or by transit in bad weather: a friend or relative outside the outage area, a library or community center, and the warming centers your city opens (check its website or non-emergency line). Write the addresses and hours by hand on the printable Our reasons to leave sheet. Agree your trigger: go if anyone cannot stay warm in the warm room with all their layers on, and go early with babies (FN-05), older adults and anyone unwell, before any sign of hypothermia (X7-01).
actions.done: Two or three heated places you can reach are on the Our reasons to leave sheet with addresses and hours, and everyone at home has agreed the trigger.

actions.title: Install a carbon monoxide alarm with battery backup
actions.why: Carbon monoxide has no smell or color, so an alarm is the only warning you will get, and it has to keep working when the power is off.
actions.how: Install a battery-powered alarm, or a plug-in one with battery backup, on every level of your home and outside each sleeping area; in a one-level apartment that means the hallway outside the bedrooms. A combination smoke and carbon monoxide alarm that meets both UL 217 and UL 2034 can do both jobs in those places, in place of a separate smoke alarm and carbon monoxide alarm. Follow the maker's instructions for where on the wall it goes. Press the test button once a month and replace the unit by the date the maker gives. If it sounds, get everyone out into fresh air and call 911 (or your local emergency number) from there.
actions.done: A carbon monoxide alarm that runs on a battery or has battery backup is installed in each place this action names, and each one sounds on its test button.
actions.apartment: Carbon monoxide can travel from a boiler room, a garage or a neighbor's appliance, so install one even if your own home is all-electric, and ask your landlord whether they provide one.

actions.title: Add the winter items to the car kit
actions.why: A car stuck in snow or in a long winter traffic jam becomes your shelter until help arrives.
actions.how: The car kit itself is the Car kit list (BG-08). From the first frost, add the winter items to it: a hat and mittens for each seat, an ice scraper and brush, a small shovel, and a bag of sand or non-clumping cat litter for grip. Keep the fuel tank near full in winter and never below half (an electric car at least half charged). If you are stranded, stay with the car and call for help. For heat, run the engine for about 10 minutes each hour with a window open a little and the exhaust pipe clear of snow, so that carbon monoxide does not build up inside.
actions.done: A hat and mittens for each seat, an ice scraper and brush, a small shovel and a bag of sand or non-clumping cat litter are in the car.

actions.title: Leave your home ready for a freeze before you go away
actions.why: A pipe that freezes and bursts in an empty home floods it, and the homes below, long before anyone notices.
actions.how: Before you go away in cold weather, leave the heat on and set no lower than 55 °F. Open the cabinet doors under the sinks so room air reaches the pipes. Unhook any hoses from outdoor faucets and store them inside. Ask a neighbor to check your home regularly while you are away, above all on the coldest days. Show them where your water shutoff valve is (HC-20), so they can shut the water off at once if a pipe freezes. This site's suggestion: leave that neighbor a key, tell management who has it and when you are back, and if your thermostat or a sensor can send a low-temperature alert to your phone, switch it on.
actions.done: Before you leave, the heat is set to 55 °F or higher, the sink cabinets are open, and a neighbor who will check your home knows where the water shutoff valve is.

actions.title: Check the whole route for winter warnings before a long drive
actions.why: Most winter warnings never arrive as an alert on your phone, so you have to look for them before you set out.
actions.how: Before a long drive in winter, look up the forecast and warnings for every place along the route, not only where you start and where you are going. The National Weather Service's list of warnings it sends to phones as Wireless Emergency Alerts includes snow squall warnings but not winter storm, blizzard or ice storm warnings, so check weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio or local news yourself. If a winter storm warning covers any part of the route, stay off the road if at all possible. If you must go, have the winter items in the car first (HC-26).
actions.done: Every driver at home has a weather app or bookmarked page on their phone that shows warnings for any place along a route.
